Authors: Hoveling LA, Bergink-Voorthuis BJ, van Vlaardingen JRG, Verhoeven RHA, Wagner AD, Soerjomataram I, Siesling S
Journal: ESMO real world data and digital oncology | DOI: 10.1016/j.esmorw.2026.100790
Published: 2026-Dec-01
PMID: 42959695



Abstract:
BACKGROUND: We analysed sex differences in global cancer incidence and mortality using a national development index to better understand how broader socioeconomic factors may contribute to or mitigate sex differences in cancer outcomes. MATERIALS AND METHODS: Cancer incidence and mortality data (2012-2017) were obtained from the International Agency for Research on Cancer, covering 43 countries for incidence and 60 for mortality. Only nonsex-specific cancers were included and categorised into 12 groups. Age-standardised incidence rates (ASIR) and age-standardised mortality rates (ASMRs) were calculated, with sex differences analysed using men-to-women ratios (MWRs). Linear regression was used to assess the association between Human Development Index (HDI) and MWRs across cancer types. RESULTS: Among the cancer types included in this study, cancers of the colorectum, stomach, and lungs showed the highest incidence and mortality. Men are 12-13 times more likely to be diagnosed with oesophageal cancer (MWR ≈ 13), over nine times more likely to die from head and neck cancers, and >6 times more likely to die from lung cancer. Thyroid cancer incidence is up to five times higher in women than in men. No clear link was found between HDI and MWRs in incidence, but HDI relates to mortality and MWRs for several cancer types, with brain and thyroid cancers showing higher male mortality, while lung cancer showing relatively higher female mortality in high-HDI countries. CONCLUSIONS: Sex differences in cancer burden vary substantially across cancer types. National development was associated with sex differences in mortality, but not incidence, suggesting that factors related to health care and survival differ more between countries with different HDIs and contribute to these differences more than exposure to risk factors, which relates more to incidence.

item.title: #2 [0/100] Living longer or living better - priorities among head and neck cancer survivors.
item.dc:creator: Thomsen A, Trigui N, Rast J, Newton-Tanzer E, Donate MG, Hoffmann M, Wiegand S

Authors: Thomsen A, Trigui N, Rast J, Newton-Tanzer E, Donate MG, Hoffmann M, Wiegand S
Journal: BMC cancer | DOI: 10.1186/s12885-026-17298-z
Published: 2026-Nov-03
PMID: 42977905



Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Head and neck cancer and its treatment can profoundly affect physical function, psychosocial well-being, and overall quality of life (QoL). As survival rates improve, integrating patient-reported outcomes and individual treatment preferences into clinical decision-making has become increasingly important. This study aimed to assess the preferences of head and neck cancer (HNC) survivors regarding QoL versus life prolongation in order to better inform patient-centered treatment decisions. METHODS: Adult head and neck cancer survivors completed validated questionnaires assessing health-related QoL (EORTC QLQ-C30), distress (Distress Thermometer), and preferences for QoL versus life prolongation (QQ questionnaire). Multivariable regression analyses were used to identify predictors of QoL and distress, while associations between patient characteristics and treatment preference were examined using group comparisons. RESULTS: The study included 207 patients (70.5% male; mean age 66.2 years). The median global health status (QLQ-C30) was 66.6, and the median distress score was 3, indicating a relatively good overall QoL and a comparatively low level of psychological distress. In multivariable analysis, lower distress and employment (both p < 0.001) as well as surgical treatment and lower comorbidity (both p < 0.05) were independently associated with better QoL. Independent predictors of distress included sex, global health status, tumor stage, educational level, and treatment modality (all p < 0.05). Regarding preferences (n = 202), 53.0% of patients prioritized QoL, 21.8% favored life prolongation, and 25.2% reported no clear preference. Preference was significantly associated with age (p = 0.035), with older patients favoring QoL, and with tumor stage (p = 0.032), with the differences between options diminishing in advanced stages. CONCLUSION: QoL in head and neck cancer survivors is shaped by both clinical and psychosocial factors. Lower distress, employment, surgical treatment, and lower comorbidity were associated with better QoL, while most patients prioritized QoL over life prolongation, particularly at older age. These findings emphasize the need to align treatment strategies with patient values, placing QoL at the center of clinical decision-making.

Authors: Jacob T, Hayat L, Krutik D, Kotz L, Carmel-Neidermann NN, Shendler G, Izkhakov E, Pestrikov T, Trejo L, Muhanna N, et al.
Journal: The Laryngoscope | DOI: 10.1002/lary.71020
Published: 2026-Nov-03
PMID: 42977881



Abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To evaluate the accuracy of preoperative ultrasound in estimating tumor size, multifocality, and extrathyroidal extension in papillary thyroid carcinoma. METHODS: A retrospective cohort study was conducted at a tertiary referral center, including patients who underwent curative surgery for papillary thyroid carcinoma between 2006 and 2022. Agreement between preoperative ultrasound-estimated and postoperative pathologic tumor size was assessed overall and across predefined size categories (≤ 1 cm, 1-2 cm, 2-3 cm, 3-4 cm, and > 4 cm). The diagnostic performance of ultrasound for detecting multifocality and extrathyroidal extension was also evaluated. RESULTS: The medical records of a total of 931 patients were reviewed. The mean sonographic and pathologic tumor sizes were 2.10 ± 1.42 cm and 1.64 ± 1.28 cm, respectively (p < 0.001). Ultrasound consistently overestimated tumor size across all groups, with the mean percentage difference rising from 6% in tumors ≤ 1 cm to 32% in tumors > 4 cm (p < 0.001). The overall mean percent difference was +15.7 ± 40.7%, indicating bias toward larger sonographic measurements. Ultrasound detection of extrathyroidal extension showed a positive predictive value of 30% and a negative predictive value of 95%; a positive predictive value of 40% and a negative predictive value of 85% for multifocality. CONCLUSION: Our findings indicate that ultrasound tends to overestimate tumor size and that it has limited predictive accuracy for multifocality and extrathyroidal extension. They demonstrate the need for caution when planning a total thyroidectomy based solely upon preoperative ultrasound findings in the absence of suspected nodal metastasis.

Authors: Ponce DM, DeFilipp Z, Ford CB, Tejura B, Lombardo MJ, Lichter DI, Chafee M, Kosuri S, Khera N, Murthy HS, et al.
Journal: Nature medicine | DOI: 10.1038/s41591-026-04686-y
Published: 2026-Nov-03
PMID: 42977758



Abstract:
Gastrointestinal (GI) microbiome disruption and impaired GI barrier integrity increase the risk of bloodstream infection (BSI) following allogeneic hematopoietic cell transplant. Here we report results from a two-cohort (open-label, n = 15; randomized, placebo-controlled, n = 45) phase 1b study of SER-155, an investigational, cultivated, multi-strain, oral live biotherapeutic designed to address GI microbiome disruption GI epithelial barrier integrity in allogeneic hematopoietic cell transplant recipients. In cohort 2, 34 of 45 participants received either SER-155 treatment (n = 20, SER-155 following microbiome conditioning with oral vancomycin), or placebo (n = 14), and subsequently received transplant. For the primary safety endpoint, SER-155 was well tolerated, with a safety profile comparable to placebo, no treatment-related serious adverse events and no infections with SER-155 species; the most common adverse events were diarrhea and nausea. Four participants in cohort 1 and four participants in cohort 2 (two participants in the SER-155 arm and two in the placebo arm) died during the study; none was attributable to SER-155. For the primary pharmacokinetic endpoint, engraftment was detected for 16 of 16 SER-155 strains, with a median of 11.5 strains detected after the first treatment course. The key secondary efficacy endpoint revealed a significantly lower incidence of BSI with SER-155 versus placebo (10.0% versus 43%; OR 0.15; 95% CI 0.01-1.13; P = 0.0423; 77% relative risk reduction). Other secondary efficacy endpoints (GI infection, acute graft-versus-host disease ≥grade 2, febrile neutropenia and a composite endpoint of BSI, GI infection or acute graft-versus-host disease) were not statistically significant. The secondary pharmacodynamic endpoint of GI domination by Enterococcus and Enterobacteriaceae spp. was not achieved. ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT04995653 .

Authors: Chen C, Hao L, Xie W, Tang R, Guo R, Zhang Z, Li J, Liang D, Jin M, Zheng Z, et al.
Journal: Nature medicine | DOI: 10.1038/s41591-026-04737-4
Published: 2026-Nov-03
PMID: 42977757



Abstract:
Menopausal hormone therapy (MHT) alleviates climacteric symptoms, yet its microbiome-wide effects and efficacy determinants remain unclear. Here we show that oral estradiol/dydrogesterone, given for 6 months to 356 perimenopausal women, improved neuroendocrine, metabolic and symptom outcomes and induced site-specific microbial remodeling. Vaginocervical and urinary niches showed the most pronounced restructuring, with moderate oral and minimal gut changes. MHT increased vaginocervical Lactobacillus crispatus and reduced Gardnerella vaginalis. Higher baseline vaginocervical L. crispatus predicted greater postintervention vaginocervical and urinary colonization and superior Female Sexual Function Index improvement. Baseline vaginocervical community types determined differential outcomes: G. vaginalis-dominated individuals shifted most toward healthier communities, whereas diversified individuals improved least. MHT efficacy also varied according to baseline gut community type: Phocaeicola vulgatus-dominated women exhibited greater hormonal responsiveness, superior clinical outcomes and were more likely to achieve 4-week rapid clinical remission than Prevotella copri-dominated women. These findings support a precision MHT framework integrating gut and vaginocervical community typing for personalized care. Chictr.org.cn ID: ChiCTR2100049768 .

Authors: Tuunanen J, Hautamäki K, Väyrynen T, Järvelä M, Korhonen V, Huotari N, Kaakinen M, Kananen J, Helakari H, Raitamaa L, et al.
Journal: Nature communications | DOI: 10.1038/s41467-026-78894-y
Published: 2026-Nov-03
PMID: 42977753



Abstract:
An age-related neurovascular impairment in nitric oxide (NO)-mediated vasodilation and reciprocal Piezo1-dependent vascular vasoconstriction may precede the accumulation of soluble brain proteins such as amyloid-β (Aβ) and disruption of brain fluid homeostasis in Alzheimer's disease (AD). Preclinical studies suggest that restoring these pathways can enhance neurofluid transport and improve cognitive outcomes. In this study (EudraCT 2021-000625-27), we investigated the effects of sublingual NO and Piezo1-targeted whole-body vibrations (WBVp) in healthy adults (n = 29) using multimodal neuroimaging and blood biomarker analysis. The combined intervention (NO+WBVp) was associated with correlating changes in brain fluid dynamics and increased blood levels of soluble brain-derived proteins (Aβ40&42, GFAP). These effects increased with age and the magnitude of NO-induced hypotension. The interventions were well tolerated under controlled experimental conditions. Overall, the findings are consistent with transient redistribution of brain-derived proteins toward circulation, suggesting a potential non-invasive approach to increase neurofluidic solute efflux in humans. Pre-specified primary endpoints, changes in circulating brain-derived protein concentrations, brain fluid imaging and brain pulsation measures, were met. Secondary outcomes included physiological analyses.

Authors: Tam K, Caxeiro G, Dunn L, Boe LA, Finnegan E, Sherman E, Xu B, Ghossein R, Cohen MA, Cracchiolo JR, et al.
Journal: Oral oncology | DOI: 10.1016/j.oraloncology.2026.108209
Published: 2026-Nov-03
PMID: 42976421



Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Neoadjuvant chemotherapy (NACT) with taxane, platinum, and cetuximab (TPC) prior to surgical resection of oral cavity squamous cell carcinoma (OCSCC) can result in dramatic decreases in tumor burden in critical anatomic subsites. We investigate the impact of TPC-based NACT on surgical morbidity and compare oncologic outcomes to a propensity-matched conventionally treated cohort. METHODS: Between 2015 and 2023, 44 patients who received TPC prior to definitive surgical resection of OCSCC were identified. Charts were retrospectively reviewed to classify the extent of resection proposed at initial presentation versus the completed surgery after NACT. Patients were classified as having undergone response-adapted surgery (RAS), standard surgery (SS), or extended surgery (ES). Surgical morbidity was quantified using a Surgical Morbidity scoring system. Oncological outcomes were compared to a propensity score-matched cohort treated with upfront primary surgery, matched on age, sex, WUHNCI, clinical T status, clinical N status and oral cavity subsite. RESULTS: Of 44 patients, 20 underwent RAS, 21 had SS, and 3 required ES. RAS patients had less extensive operations and decreased morbidity: 12 total or subtotal glossectomies were reduced to hemi- or partial glossectomies, 9 cheek flaps and 5 mandibulotomies were avoided, and 2 segmental mandibulectomies were converted to marginal mandibulectomies. Four received fasciocutaneous rather than osteocutaneous free flaps, and 2 no longer required a free flap. A trend toward improved 2-year DSS in the RAS versus SS group did not reach significance (p = 0.089). TPC NACT patients had improved 5-year overall survival compared with propensity-matched controls (73 % vs. 40 %, p = 0.003). Disease-specific survival was also higher in the NACT cohort (75 % vs. 49 %, p = 0.013). There were trends toward improved local and regional recurrence-free probability in the NACT cohort, though neither reached statistical significance. CONCLUSIONS: TPC NACT prior to definitive surgery for OCSCC was associated with reduced surgical morbidity. RAS patients underwent less morbid surgeries while maintaining comparable survival. There was no detrimental impact on survival in NACT patients compared to matched non-NACT patients.

Authors: Collins-McGowan S, Aligne CA, McDermott K, Cabral C, Ramos Benitez AP, Lomack M, Mayo N
Journal: PloS one | DOI: 10.1371/journal.pone.0361893
Published: 2026-01-01
PMID: 42976218



Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Literacy is an important social determinant of health. Failure to develop emergent literacy skills before kindergarten is a risk factor for academic failure, poverty, incarceration, and early death. Reading comprehension depends on both language comprehension and alphabetic decoding skills. The Home Literacy Environment literature tends to focus on reading aloud to develop oral language but less is known about letter-themed tools. DESIGN: Our hypothesis was that letter-themed toys and books would be acceptable to all families but that lower socio-economic status (SES) households would be less likely to have them. Using methods of Community Based Participatory Research, 3 caregivers with young children living in the City of Rochester, NY, completed IRB training and provided cultural context for decisions throughout this study. We surveyed a convenience sample of 156 caregivers at 10 community events. We showed a poster with pictures of alphabet-themed toys and asked caregivers to count how many they had in the home. ZIP code was used as a proxy for SES. RESULTS: We surveyed 156 caregivers, excluding 13 responses because of missing information. Of the 143 remaining, 139 (97.2%) thought it was important that a child know most of the alphabet letters before kindergarten. 1 in 4 of our respondents didn't have a single literacy toy in their home and an additional 1 in 6 had only one. We calculated a p value of 0.0004 for the hypothesis that there is a difference by SES in the number of these items in the home. CONCLUSIONS: Our results are consistent with the hypothesis that joyful letter-themed tools are acceptable to parents in general but that low-SES households are less likely to have them. Closing the gap in early alphabet exposure could contribute to reducing inequities in school success and lifelong health.

Authors: Aydın Çetin EZ, Özmen B
Journal: PloS one | DOI: 10.1371/journal.pone.0362074
Published: 2026-01-01
PMID: 42976146



Abstract:
UNLABELLED: This randomized clinical trial aimed to compare the effects of cryotherapy, anesthetic spray, and gel on pain, anxiety, physiological responses, taste acceptability, and treatment compliance in children aged 7-10 years undergoing their first dental treatment. 100 healthy children were randomly allocated into four groups: 10% lidocaine spray, 20% benzocaine gel, cryotherapy with distilled water cooled to +4 °C, and lidocaine spray cooled to +4 °C. Following topical application, buccal infiltration anesthesia was administered. Anxiety, pain, and physiological responses were assessed using the Modified Dental Anxiety Scale and Facial Image Scale, Wong-Baker FACES Pain Rating Scale, and pulse-oximeter. Taste acceptability and treatment compliance were evaluated using a three-point Hedonic Scale and the FRANKL Scale. Repeated Measures ANOVA, Mann-Whitney U, and Kruskal-Wallis tests were applied. No significant differences were observed among the groups in anxiety, pain, pulse rate, oxygen saturation, or taste acceptability (p > 0.05). Pulse rate increased from the pre-operative to the post-operative period in all groups (p = 0.006), with no significant group × time interaction. FRANKL scores were significantly higher in the cryotherapy-distilled water group compared with the gel and cooled-spray groups (p = 0.001), a finding considered exploratory. Pain and anxiety outcomes following cryotherapy did not differ significantly from those of the topical anesthetic agents, while treatment compliance was higher, suggesting that cryotherapy may be a promising non-pharmacological option, pending confirmation in non-inferiority trials. TRIAL REGISTRATION: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT07198022.

Authors: Islam JY, Commaroto SA, McGee-Avila JK, Lin YC, Guo Y, Turner K, Alishahi Tabriz A, Camacho-Rivera M, Portillo-Romero AJ, D'Souza G, et al.
Journal: Cancer epidemiology, biomarkers & prevention : a publication of the American Association for Cancer Research, cosponsored by the American Society of Preventive Oncology | DOI: 10.1158/1055-9965.EPI-26-0622
Published: 2026-Nov-03
PMID: 42975869



Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Although a rare malignancy, anal cancer incidence is increasing with a growing proportion diagnosed at advanced stages. Our objective was to evaluate factors associated with advanced stage-at-diagnosis (stage 3+) of squamous cell carcinoma of the anus (SCCA) among men and women with and without HIV. METHODS: We analyzed U.S. National Cancer Database data (2004-2020) for patients aged 18-89 years with SCCA (ICD-O-3: C210-C218). The outcome was advanced stage at diagnosis (stage 3/4). Stratified by sex, we assessed associations with demographics, HIV status, healthcare access (facility type, insurance), and geographic factors using hierarchical multivariable Poisson regression to estimate adjusted prevalence ratios (aPR) and 95% confidence intervals (CI). RESULTS: Among 36,389 patients with SCCA, 2,600 (7.1%) were living with HIV and 42% were diagnosed at stage 3-4. Women without HIV were more likely to be diagnosed at an advanced stage compared to men without HIV (aPR: 1.20, 95% CI: 1.05-1.37). Among both sexes, NH-Black race (aPR: 1.09, 95% CI: 1.04-1.14), being uninsured (aPR: 1.31, 95% CI: 1.23-1.39), Medicaid insurance (aPR: 1.19, 95% CI: 1.13-1.24), and residing in the least-educated zip codes (aPR: 1.09, 95% CI: 1.04-1.15) were associated with advanced-stage diagnosis. Among women, advanced-stage diagnosis was associated with NH-Asian race (aPR: 1.23, 95% CI: 1.06-1.42). HIV status was not independently associated. CONCLUSIONS: Correlates of advanced-stage SCCA differed by sex; living with HIV was not associated with advanced-stage presentation. IMPACT: These findings identify NH-Black and NH-Asian women, uninsured individuals, and Medicaid enrollees as populations more likely to be diagnosed with advanced-stage SCCA.
